title: Fin‐Tuning Evolution: Integration, Constraint, and the Ecomechanics of Shark Median Fins
content:
We quantify median fin shape in 480 shark species (∼88% of extant diversity) using a standardized illustration dataset. We test how evolutionary integration and modularity shape locomotor morphology across shark ecotypes. Results show strong variation in disparity, integration, and evolutionary rates among bauplans and ecological gradients, with evidence that phenotypic integration constrains diversification. Median fin morphology also varies with depth and trophic level, and the anal fin may functionally complement dorsal fins.


ABSTRACT

Phenotypic integration and modularity are central to morphological evolution, particularly in coordinated locomotor systems. In vertebrates, evolutionary integration in the locomotor apparatus is hypothesized to both facilitate and constrain morphological diversification, depending on the system in question. The median fins are ideal for studying patterns of evolutionary integration and modularity, combining developmental linkage with variable functional coupling. However, the function of the median fins of cartilaginous fishes remains incompletely understood. Using a comprehensive, standardized dataset of scientific illustrations, we quantify median fin shape and aspect ratio for 480 shark species (∼88% of extant shark diversity). We find variation in levels of disparity, integration, and evolutionary rates among shark ecotypes and bauplans, indicating that phenotypic integration can limit diversification in locomotor morphology. Median fin shape also varies across ecological gradients, including water depth and trophic level. Together, our results suggest that the shark anal fin may mirror the function of the dorsal fins—potentially reducing functional demands on the remaining median fins and facilitating the evolution of diverse morphologies.
